newsitem.title: USA: July wholesale inventories up, sales strong.
newsitem.headline: July wholesale inventories up, sales strong.

text.p: Inventories of unsold goods on wholesalers' shelves grew only slightly in July as sales posted their strongest rise in nearly two years, the Commerce Department said Tuesday.

Overall inventories were up 0.1 percent to a seasonally adjusted $259.45 billion -- less than the 0.3 percent increase forecast by Wall Street economists -- following a revised 0.2 percent gain in June.
Previously, the department said June inventories were unchanged from May.

The biggest increases in inventories in July were in lumber and construction materials, furniture and new cars and parts. Sales of new cars were weaker in July, which likely accounts for some of the increase in supplies of new cars, though carmakers reported a rebound in August sales.
Commerce said auto inventories increased 1.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $28.33 billion in July after rising 1.5 percent in June.

The report suggested that sales were strong enough to support a pickup in production of many hard goods as the second half of the year began. That already is showing up in a brisker pace of business for many manufacturing industries.
During July, total wholesale sales increased 2.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted $203.21 billion -- the biggest monthly gain since a 2.7 percent rise in August 1994.
That followed a revised fractional 0.1 percent rise in June that originally was reported as a 0.3 percent gain.
As a result, the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to deplete inventories at the current sales pace, dropped to 1.28 months' worth from 1.31 months' in June.

The department said it was the lowest sales ratio since August 1994, when it also was down to 1.28 months' worth, a further indication that there was room for companies to gear up production lines in coming months to meet demand.
